title: the thoughts that aren't you
tomorrow: feet on the floor, hands on the knees

cards: Here's a thought for you: you left the stove on. Did you? Probably not.
But for half a second, your stomach believed it. Thoughts arrive like that all day, uninvited, sounding completely sure of themselves.
One large study checked in with people through their phones, at random moments, and asked what they were doing and what they were thinking about. Their minds were somewhere else almost half the time.
Two words help with that. Not you. Weather.

teach.h: IT IS NOTHING JOINTED; IT FLOWS.
teach.b: In 1890, William James described something everyone lives with and few had put well: the stream of thought. Consciousness, he wrote, "is nothing jointed; it flows." A river, not a row of boxes.
Thoughts come and go on it, and you didn't send most of them. Nearly two thousand years earlier, the Greek teacher Epictetus, who was born enslaved, came at it another way.

In an old translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The trouble is less the event than the judgment we add on top of it, and that judgment is ours to examine.
Many Buddhist teachers, especially in the Tibetan tradition, use a picture you may like: the mind is like the sky, and thoughts are like weather. Clouds, storms, bright spells. They move through.
The sky isn't the clouds, and it isn't harmed by them. A stream, an opinion you can question, weather in the sky.
Three different pictures, and each one treats a thought as something that happens in you, not the whole of you.

how: In many forms of meditation, people let thoughts come and go without following them, often noting them simply as "thinking" and returning to the breath; Stoic practice examines the judgments behind troubling thoughts instead.

games.q: your friend is upset about a rude email. where would Epictetus point first?
o: at the opinion your friend added to it.
at the person who sent it.
games.why: "men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." the email happened; the judgment is the part that's yours to examine.

practice: Here's the practice. The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle.
When a thought shows up, name it quietly: thinking. Don't follow it, and don't fight it. Watch it move on, the way weather does.
Then you're back here, in the body that's breathing.

wordCard.voice: Thoughts. Things that happen in you, like weather. Not the whole of you. Eighth word.

orig.note: Greek, dogmata: Epictetus's word in Enchiridion 5 for the opinions that disturb us. English dogma comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: let it pass. Not every thought that sounds sure of itself gets a vote. Day eight.
